To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) wave V latencies increased with increasing rate in both age groups, (b) wave V amplitude decreased with increasing rate in the older adults, and (c) the older adults had significantly smaller amplitudes than the young adults.
The latencies of waves I and of V, and of the I-V interval, increased with increasing click rate, whereas the amplitudes of these waves decreased.

1) The ABR is a robust response that is relatively insensitive to click rate in both young and older adults; 2) The ABR to clicks at rates up to 75 Hz is not affected by aging; 3) The ABR at 100 Hz is also unaffected by aging; and 4) The ABRs to click rates of 200 Hz and above are not affected by aging.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the auditory system and its responses to sound.
the effects of aging on auditory brainstem responses to high click rates.
the effects of aging on the auditory system and the development of aural rehabilitation programs for older adults with hearing loss.

there is no significant difference between young and older adults in terms of ABR wave I-V latency and I-V amplitude.
the ABR wave I latency and amplitude are not affected by age, and the ABR wave V latency is affected by age.
the auditory brainstem response wave I is not affected by aging.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
aging effects are most likely to be observed when the ABR is evoked by a stimulus with a high rate of repetition.
aging affects ABR wave V latency, but not ABR wave I latency, at short forward-maskeing intervals, but not at high click rates.
wave V latency increases and wave V amplitude decreases with increasing click rate.
The main takeaway from our work is that
wave I amplitude is substantially reduced in older adults.
the ABR is a very useful tool to study the aging auditory system, especially if wave I can be measured reliably.
the ABR can be reliably recorded in older adults using a tympanic membrane electrode, high-level clicks, and click rate as an independent variable.
